 Inspiration The best time to visit the Maldives: a guide to weather, rainy season and the cheapest months
 From sun-drenched winter escapes to swimming with manta rays, here’s how to choose the best time to visit the Maldives By Anna Prendergast and Scott Campbell November 6, 2026 Getty Images Some destinations are gorgeous year-round, but when is the best time to go to the Maldives to make the most of the weather in this dream destination? Whether your goal is to relax with perfect sunshine, see the best marine life, or just want to avoid crowds, planning in advance is important ahead of a trip to somewhere like the Maldives.
 Chances are, you want to go to the Maldives because you've seen how beautiful it is. Dotted like ink blots in the clear, tropical waters of the Indian Ocean, the Maldives is an archipelago made up of more than 1,000 islands, 200 of which are inhabited. Historically a honeymoon destination , the best hotels in the Maldives have shifted the destination up a gear, opening it up further to the realms of solo travel and multi-generational holidays. Between the consistently hot weather, unspoilt sandy beaches , high-design hotels and award-winning restaurants, it’s hard to find fault with this small but mighty contender for winter sunshine.
 But there's no denying that it's a bucket list destination for many, so it's understandable that you'd want to plan as much as possible to find the perfect time to go. Here's everything you need to know about the best time to visit the Maldives.
 The Maldives is home to more than 1,000 islands
 AscentXmedia When is the best time to go to the Maldives?
 There’s no bad time to visit the Maldives, it really does have it all: upwards of eight hours of sun per day, average temperatures of around 28°C, an ocean teeming with wildlife and some of the smartest hotels in the world.
 But for most travellers, the best time to visit is between December and April, during the dry season, when lower humidity and relatively little rainfall bring bright blue skies, long sunny days and still, balmy evenings. January, February and March are particularly reliable for sunshine, making them the most popular months for a winter escape.
 The wetter southwest monsoon typically arrives in May and lasts until October or November, bringing more frequent showers, stronger winds and occasionally rougher seas – however, rainfall is often short-lived, and there can still be plenty of sunshine between showers.
 For scuba divers and snorkellers, underwater visibility is generally excellent during the dry season, particularly on the eastern sides of the atolls. Those hoping to encounter manta rays, however, may find the wetter months more rewarding, especially in Baa Atoll, where plankton-rich waters attract large numbers of the animals between May and November.
 April and November are considered the shoulder season, when travellers can sometimes find lower room rates while still enjoying warm temperatures and plenty of sunshine. The weather can be less predictable, particularly in November, but the potential savings make both months worth considering.
 When is the cheapest time to visit the Maldives?
 The cheapest time to visit the Maldives is during the low season, generally between May and October, when hotel rates can drop substantially. Resorts often offer incentives such as complimentary nights, meal plan upgrades and discounted transfers, making some of the country’s most luxurious properties considerably more affordable.
 You do risk cloudy days, tropical downpours and occasionally strong winds, but temperatures remain comfortably in the high 20s, and sunshine is still common.
 A few extra tips to save on price: choose a resort accessible by speedboat rather than seaplane to avoid expensive transfers, look out for introductory offers at newly opened hotels and consider travelling outside school holidays. Booking a half-board or all-inclusive package can also help keep costs down, particularly on private islands where restaurants are operated exclusively by the resort.
 Winter brings some of the clearest weather in the Maldives
 Getty Images What's winter like in the Maldives?
 Whether you’ve got your PADI or you just fancy a fun dive, dipping beneath the archipelago’s surface is a magical experience. From the native corals, colourful anemones and otherworldly nudibranchs to the docile sea turtles, swooping manta rays and curious (but harmless) whale sharks, the excellent visibility here makes it one of the best places to witness marine life in its natural habitat. Many resorts have in-house marine biologists who enable budding conservationists of every age to learn more about the environment and help make a positive impact on it. Indulgent infinity pools and white sandy sweeps descending into shallow, sparkling waters are primed for a paddle; secluded picnic spots and private terraces make for the finest of dining experiences; overwater villas make even your down-time up-market; wellness centres and bespoke spa experiences help you to fully embrace the go-slow pace.
 What are the Maldives like during Christmas and New Year?
 During the festive season in the Maldives, Santa doesn’t use a sledge – he arrives by seaplane. And despite the islands’ laid-back atmosphere, many resorts know how to put on a celebration, with elaborate festive programmes, Christmas dinners on the beach and New Year’s Eve parties beneath the stars.
 At resorts such as Gili Lankanfushi , The Nautilus and JOALI , previous festive programmes have included Christmas tree-lighting ceremonies, children’s activities, special dining experiences and visits from Father Christmas. From open-air Christmas films to spectacular New Year’s Eve celebrations, even those hoping to escape the usual holiday-season obligations may find themselves getting into the festive spirit.
 Christmas and New Year are also among the most expensive times to visit the Maldives. Many resorts introduce minimum-stay requirements and compulsory gala dinners, while the most sought-after villas can sell out months in advance. For families and couples planning a festive escape, early booking is essential.
 When is the rainy season in the Maldives?
 The rainy season typically starts in April or May and lasts until October or November. The rain is due to the South West monsoon, which causes stormier conditions that can last for days. However, you can expect plenty of dry and sunny periods to occur during this time too.
 Rainy season can be good for spotting certain marine life, like mantarays
 Getty Images When is the best time to dive in the Maldives?
 You can go diving year-round in the Maldives. The best underwater visibility and weather can be expected from December to April. You can expect to see everything from manta rays to reef sharks.
 Where to stay in the Maldives
 Truly, it's hard to find a bad resort in this slice of paradise. Where you choose to stay will depend on your budget – but there are plenty of options for everyone.
 Sea villa at Soneva Secret, Maldives Stevie Mann Soneva Secret
 Soneva has spent nearly three decades perfecting its particular brand of barefoot luxury, but Soneva Secret, its most intimate Maldivian outpost, takes things to rather extraordinary lengths. Hidden away in the remote Haa Dhaalu Atoll, where the ocean stretches uninterrupted in every direction, the resort has just 14 villas, each assigned a private chef and a small team of dedicated hosts. The residences are enormous, with retractable roofs that open above the beds for stargazing, private pools and waterslides that plunge straight into the lagoon. There’s even a floating villa, accessible only by boat, for those who find an ordinary private island insufficiently secluded. To dine, guests can zipline to Out of This World, a restaurant perched above the sea, or summon their chef to prepare dinner in the privacy of their villa. There’s a chocolate room, an ice cream parlour and a marine biology programme that makes a compelling case for occasionally leaving the sun lounger.
 Book now at Soneva.com KENSEET Four Seasons Resort Maldives at Kuda Huraa
 The Maldives has spent the past decade competing to build ever bigger, shinier and more extravagant resorts, but Kuda Huraa, which opened in 1998, has little interest in keeping up. Its charm lies in its resemblance to a traditional Maldivian village, with sandy lanes winding between thatched bungalows, hibiscus hedges and flowering frangipani. The 96 villas and bungalows have been updated over the years, but the island has retained its easy, lived-in atmosphere. It’s also one of the archipelago’s best addresses for surfing, with six breaks nearby and instructors on hand for everyone from first-timers to seasoned wave riders.
 Book now at Booking.com GEORG ROSKE Patina Maldives, Fari Islands
 There’s an artful sensibility to Patina Maldives that sets it apart from the archipelago’s more conventional castaway retreats. Designed by Brazilian architect Marcio Kogan of Studio MK27, the resort occupies one of the Fari Islands in North Malé Atoll, a 45-minute speedboat ride from the airport. Art is everywhere, from James Turrell’s Skyspace installation to sculptures scattered among the gardens, while the Fari Marina Village brings a rare sense of community to an otherwise secluded island escape, with boutiques, restaurants and a beach club shared with neighbouring resorts. There’s an impressive culinary line-up here, too, including plant-based dining at Roots and Japanese-Nordic cooking at Kōen.
 Book now at Booking.com A. Shuau / @obofili The Standard, Huruvalhi Maldives
 The Standard has never been particularly interested in following the rules of conventional luxury hospitality, and its Maldivian outpost is no exception. On Huruvalhi Island in Raa Atoll, the usual ingredients of a tropical escape – overwater villas, powdery beaches and an impossibly blue lagoon – come with disco balls in the bathrooms and a social calendar that extends well beyond sunset. The 115 villas all have private pools and direct access to the water, while the resort’s house reef provides ample opportunity for snorkelling without venturing far from shore.
 Book now at Booking.com Ralf Tooten The St. Regis Maldives Vommuli Resort
 Few hotels in the Maldives make quite such an architectural statement as The St. Regis Maldives Vommuli Resor – there’s a whale shark-shaped bar perched above the lagoon, a lobster-inspired spa and a striking collection of overwater villas arranged to resemble a manta ray when viewed from above. The 77 villas are suitably extravagant, with private pools, marble bathrooms and the brand’s signature butler service, while the resort’s tropical interior conceals a surprisingly lush jungle of palms and banyan trees.
 Book now at Booking.com Centara Grand Lagoon Maldives
 Opened in April 2025, Centara Grand Lagoon occupies a reclaimed island in North Malé Atoll, where sleek, semicircular overwater villas curve around private infinity pools and steps descend into luminous shallows. Just 30 minutes by speedboat from the airport, it’s an appealing choice for shorter stays, with 142 villas and rooms ranging from beachfront hideaways to three-bedroom overwater residences with slides into the sea. Families can also cross a bridge to neighbouring Centara Mirage Lagoon, where a water park, lazy river and children’s facilities await.
 Book now at Booking.com Anna is a freelance journalist and editor covering travel, sustainability and social issues for Condé Nast Traveller, How To Spend It, The Independent, Stylist and Glamour. Having lived in Melbourne, Barcelona and the Peloponnese, she now writes from her home in Brixton in between weekends spent scuba diving and camping.
